# Building Reliability Together: Why SLOs Matter

When users rely on your service, they expect it to be there — fast, dependable, and invisible in its reliability. But how do you make sure everyone in your company, from engineers to executives, is speaking the same language about what “reliable” really means?

At SurveySparrow, we learned that defining and measuring reliability in clear, shared terms doesn’t just prevent outages — it brings teams together, sharpens our focus, and ultimately delivers a better experience for our users.

Here’s how we turned reliability from a technical afterthought into a core part of our culture, and why SLOs became the foundation for building trust — inside and out.

## The Universal Challenge: How Good Is “Good Enough”?

Imagine you run a restaurant. How would you know if your service is satisfying customers? You might track metrics like average wait time, food quality ratings, or how often orders are correct. These measurements help everyone — from chefs to servers to managers — understand if they’re delivering the experience customers expect.

> Software services face the same fundamental question: How do we know if our service is working well enough for our users?

Before we refined our approach at SurveySparrow, answering this question was surprisingly difficult:

- **No Shared Standard:** When a customer reported that surveys were “loading slowly,” what did that mean? 2 seconds? 10 seconds? And was this within acceptable thresholds?
- **Limited Ownership:** Development teams built features but relied on specialists to handle performance monitoring, creating knowledge silos and delayed responses.
- **Centralized Observability:** Our SRE team can become a bottleneck, if only they are responsible for monitoring and fixing performance issues across all services as we scaled.

We needed a way to translate technical metrics into a language everyone could understand and act upon — something that connected directly to user experience while empowering individual teams to own their service performance end-to-end.

## Service Levels: A Universal Language

Think of service levels like a commitment between your business and your customers. Just as a pizza place might promise “delivery in 30 minutes or it’s free,” digital services need clear, measurable standards too — _penalty and the severity of SLO breach don’t need to be same as the pizza example :)_

At its simplest, a service level answers three questions:

1. What aspect of our service matters to users? (e.g., survey response time)
2. How good should it be? (e.g., under 2 seconds)
3. How often should we meet this standard? (e.g., 99.5% of the time)

By defining these parameters, we create a shared understanding that bridges departments:

- **Product Teams** understand what features truly matter to users
- **Engineering Teams** know where to focus reliability efforts
- **Support Teams** can communicate clearly about system performance

The best part? This approach isn’t just about preventing problems — it helps us systematically improve the user experience over time.

## The Service Level Framework: Making the Invisible Visible

We adopted a simple framework that makes service quality tangible for everyone:

- **Service Level Indicator (SLI):** A measurement of what users care about. For SurveySparrow, this includes how quickly surveys load, whether responses save successfully, or if reports generate correctly.
- **Service Level Objective (SLO):** A target for how good the service should be. For example: “99.9% of survey responses should save successfully” or “95% of reports should generate in under 3 seconds.”
- **Error Budget:** The acceptable room for imperfection. If your SLO is 99.9% success, your error budget is 0.1% — giving you space to innovate and take calculated risks without compromising the overall user experience.

This framework makes reliability discussions concrete. Instead of vague statements like “the system seems slow today,” we can say “we’re consuming our error budget too quickly this week” and take action before users notice.

## From Concept to Reality: Our Implementation Journey

## 1\. Focusing on What Users Actually Care About

We started by identifying the most important user journeys in SurveySparrow:

- Creating and editing surveys
- Responding to surveys
- Generating and viewing reports
- Managing contacts and distributions

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1000/1*VF8mANQnmYJDMCd2a5V90g.png)

Each team can specify as many critical SLIs as they want

For each journey, we asked: What makes this a good experience for users? Speed? Reliability? Accuracy? This helped us define what “good” looks like from the user’s perspective.

## 2\. Measuring What Matters in Simple Terms

For each important journey, we defined two simple concepts:

- **Valid Events:** Every time a user tries to do something important — like submit a survey response.
- **Good Events:** When that action succeeds quickly and correctly.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1000/1*P2NtZF9Za9vPDmjHwZitPg.png)

SLO for an API’s Error Rate featuring valid error codes as well as query for all error codes to consider

Our service level is simply the percentage of good events compared to all valid events over time. For example, if 995 out of 1000 survey submissions succeed within our target time, that’s a 99.5% service level.

## 3\. Setting Realistic Targets

For example, you can establish targets like:

- **Availability:** 99.9% of attempts to submit responses should succeed (no errors).
- **Speed:** 99% of submissions should complete in under 1 second.

For latency SLOs, we set our default target at the 99th percentile of our existing latency data (i.e. 1% of requests are taking longer than the said target).

## 4\. Establishing Clear Accountability with SLO Reporting

To maintain visibility and accountability, we implemented a weekly reporting system for SLO performance:

- **Weekly SLO Reports:** Each Monday, all teams receive an email summarizing SLO performance across services. This report highlights trends and shares current status with all relevant stakeholders, ensuring everyone has a shared understanding of service health.
- **Team-Driven Resolution:** Teams maintain continuous visibility into their SLOs and proactively address any breaches, with the weekly report serving as a checkpoint for broader awareness. SLO Breaches are a sign of a problem and should be addressed by the team that owns the service before it quickly escalates — Repeated or persistent SLO breaches are automatically escalated to stakeholders and leadership to ensure accountability and appropriate resource allocation for resolution.
- **Fast Burn Alerts:** For critical services, we use fast burn alerts that trigger when error budgets are being consumed too quickly, even before an SLO breach occurs. This gives teams early warning to investigate and address potential issues, is often more informative and earlier than SLO compliance threshold is completely crossed

This approach ensures visibility into reliability issues without creating unnecessary overhead or rigid processes.

## 5\. Making It Scalable with Infrastructure as Code

As we expanded our approach across dozens of services, manually setting up SLOs and alerts would have quickly become unmanageable. Instead, we made everything programmable using Infrastructure as Code (Terraform):

- SLO definitions (what we measure and targets)
- Alert policies (when to notify and who gets notified, for example, SLO breaches)
- Notification channels (where alerts go, like a Slack channel for each team)

This approach had several benefits:

- **Consistency:** Every team follows the same patterns and practices
- **Version Control:** Changes are documented, reviewed, and reversible

By codifying our reliability standards, we ensured consistent measurement across our entire platform without creating additional work for teams.

## Results: A Transformed Organization

The impact of implementing service levels went beyond just metrics. It fundamentally changed how we work:

- **Engineering Agility:** Teams now have clear reliability guardrails, enabling them to move fast while maintaining service quality.
- **Distributed Ownership:** Each team owns their service reliability end-to-end, with direct access to their SLO data and tooling.
- **Shared Understanding:** From SRE to engineering, everyone now speaks the same language about service health.

What was once a specialized concern has become a shared responsibility. Teams are empowered to own their service performance, leading to faster improvements and better user experiences.

## Lessons from our journey

If you’re considering implementing service levels in your organization, a few key lessons from our experience:

- **Start with the user perspective.** Define what matters to them, not what’s easiest to measure.
- **Keep it simple.** A few well-chosen metrics are better than dozens of complex ones.
- **Create a common language.** The greatest value comes when everyone — technical and non-technical — understands and uses service levels in their work.
- **Evolve over time.** Your service level objectives should grow with your product and user expectations.

At SurveySparrow, we continue to refine our approach. We’re extending service levels to our frontend experience, exploring new ways to measure what matters most to users, and using these insights to prioritize our roadmap.

## Conclusion: Building Reliability Together

One of the most powerful outcomes of adopting service levels has been breaking down silos between teams. What was once a technical conversation limited to engineering has become a shared organizational priority with a common language.

By establishing clear, measurable service levels, we’ve created a foundation for making better decisions together, keeping users happy, and continuously improving our platform. After all, reliability isn’t just a technical metric — it’s the foundation of trust between SurveySparrow and our users.

The real power of service levels isn’t in the implementation details — it’s in creating a shared understanding that helps everyone contribute to delivering exceptional user experiences, every time.
